result.summary: Ulysses buries Elpenor, and Circe warns him about the Sirens, Scylla, Charybdis and the cattle of the sun. He passes the Sirens bound to the mast and loses six men to Scylla. His crew then slaughter the sun-god's cattle, Jove destroys the ship, and Ulysses alone drifts to Calypso's island.

scenes.title: Funeral of Elpenor
scenes.summary: Back on Aeaea, Ulysses and his men burn Elpenor's body and raise a cairn topped with his oar.

scenes.title: Circe's Warnings
scenes.summary: Circe feasts the men, then privately tells Ulysses about the Sirens, the Wandering rocks, Scylla, Charybdis and the Thrinacian cattle. Ulysses relays the plan to his men.
scenes.stakes: Ulysses and his crew risk death from the Sirens, Scylla, Charybdis and the sun-god's wrath.

scenes.title: The Sirens
scenes.summary: With the crew's ears waxed and Ulysses bound to the mast, they pass the Sirens, who offer knowledge.
scenes.stakes: Ulysses risks being lured to his death by the Sirens' song.

scenes.title: Scylla and Charybdis
scenes.summary: Ulysses steers through the Straits, hides the Scylla threat, and watches Scylla seize six men.
scenes.stakes: The ship and all the crew could be destroyed by Charybdis or Scylla.

scenes.title: The Cattle Slaughtered
scenes.summary: Eurylochus persuades the men to land on Thrinacia. Starving after a month, they kill the sun's cattle while Ulysses sleeps.
scenes.stakes: The crew risk the sun-god's vengeance and loss of any chance of homecoming.

scenes.title: The Sun Demands Vengeance
scenes.summary: Ulysses finds the crime done. Lampetie tells the sun, who threatens Jove, who promises to wreck the ship. Portents appear.

scenes.title: Shipwreck and Return to Calypso
scenes.summary: Jove destroys the ship and drowns the crew. Ulysses survives on the mast, escapes Charybdis by the fig tree, and reaches Calypso's island.
scenes.stakes: Ulysses is the sole survivor and could drown or be swallowed by Charybdis.

scenes.title: End of the Tale
scenes.summary: Ulysses stops his story, since he already told of Calypso.

notable_quotes.reason: The Sirens' tempting call to Ulysses.
Ulysses calls the loss of men to Scylla his most sickening sight.
Closes the tale of his wanderings.

analysis.text: The book tests leadership and discipline: Ulysses' cunning gets him past the Sirens, but his crew's disobedience destroys them.
The route through the Straits and Sicily reflects Greek sailors' knowledge of western waters, later tied to real places.

legacy.text: 'Between Scylla and Charybdis' became a proverb for being caught between two dangers.
The Sirens became a lasting image of dangerous temptation in art and literature, and gave us the word 'siren'.

fun_facts.text: Ulysses is told that the Argo alone passed the Wandering rocks, showing the Odyssey knew an earlier Argonaut tale.

language_notes.text: "Die twice, to other people's once": having died in visiting Hades and then dying again naturally, they will have experienced death two times.
"Heaven itself will recall it to your recollection": a god will put these instructions in your mind when needed.
"Cross piece" is the horizontal spar or beam on the mast; the numeral 99 is a footnote marker.
Amphitrite is the sea goddess, wife of Neptune; here her name stands for the sea itself.
"Ambrosia" is the food of the gods, said to keep them immortal; here doves carry it to Jove.
The Argo was Jason's ship, sailing from Aetes' land to fetch the Golden Fleece; Juno (the Greek Hera) favoured Jason.
Erebus is the dark region of the underworld, so the cave faces west toward the gloom of the dead.
Crataiis is named as Scylla's mother; calling on her is meant to restrain her daughter.
"Dead aft" means blowing straight from behind the stern, pushing the ship directly forward.
The "two Sirens" are the pair of singing creatures Circe described; the number 102 is a translator's footnote marker, not part of the story.
"The sun-god son of Hyperion" is Helios, the sun. Hyperion is his father in this telling, so the phrase is a roundabout name for the sun.
"Achaean" means Greek. Homer uses Achaeans, Argives and Danaans interchangeably for the Greeks who fought at Troy.
"Exhorted" means urged or encouraged strongly.
"Give you the slip" means escape control. "Hug the rock" means steer close to the cliff, away from the whirlpool.
The fisherman's spear is tipped with a hollow ox horn, which keeps the line from being cut by the fish's teeth or bite while hauling it up.
The Wandering Rocks, Scylla and Charybdis were the perils Circe described earlier; Ulysses has just survived them, losing six men to Scylla.
Teiresias, the dead Theban seer, warned Ulysses in the underworld not to harm the sun's cattle; Circe repeated the warning.
"Watches of the flying night" means the divisions of the night, which pass quickly; a watch was a set period of duty.
"Unpropitious" means unfavourable; the gods are not disposed to help.
"Behests" are commands; Eurylochus cleverly treats night as an authority to be obeyed.
"Third watch" means roughly the middle of the night, when the stars have visibly moved.
Barley-meal was sprinkled on animals before sacrifice; the men improvise with oak leaves, a sign of their makeshift, irregular rite.
Thigh bones wrapped in fat were burned as the gods' share in a proper Greek sacrifice; the men imitate this rite.
"Square accounts" means pay what is owed; here, make compensation for the slaughtered cattle.
"Shiver" means to shatter into fragments, not to tremble.
Mercury (the Greek Hermes) is the gods' messenger, so he could relay what was said among the gods to Calypso.
A backstay is a rope supporting the mast; here it is made of ox-hide thong, which Ulysses uses to bind mast and keel.
Scylla and Charybdis were the monster and whirlpool on either side of a narrow strait, which Ulysses passed earlier in this book.
"Ogygian" describes Ogygia, Calypso's island, where Ulysses was kept for years.

context_notes.text: Elpenor was the crewman who fell from Circe's roof and died; Ulysses met his ghost in Hades, who begged for burial.
A cairn with an oar on top was a fitting memorial for a sailor, marking his grave.
The Sirens were creatures whose irresistible song lured sailors to their deaths.
The Thrinacian island belongs to the sun-god, whose sacred cattle are never to be harmed; this sets up later disaster.
The Sirens promise knowledge of the Trojan War and of the future. They tempt Ulysses with his own fame, and the song is fatal to those who linger.
Circe had told Ulysses that fighting Scylla was useless. His armour is a defiant, human reaction to that advice.
Scylla and Charybdis guard a narrow strait. Scylla is a six-headed rock-dwelling monster, and Charybdis a whirlpool that swallows the sea three times a day.
Hyperion is the sun-god, here called the sun; his sacred herds on Thrinacia must not be harmed.
Jove (the Greek Zeus) is king of the gods and controls storms; his gale keeps the men trapped on the island.
"Rosy-fingered Dawn" is a stock Homeric phrase marking the start of a new day.
The sun god (Hyperion) owned sacred cattle on the island. Ulysses' men swore not to touch them, but broke the oath when starving.
Thunderbolts are Jove's weapon (the Greek Zeus). Fire and brimstone means burning sulphur, associated with lightning strikes.

literary_notes.text: "Rosy-fingered Dawn" is a recurring Homeric epithet marking the start of a new day.
The Sirens' sweet song brings death; beauty is the lure of destruction.
Vivid details of twelve feet, six necks and triple rows of teeth make Scylla a horrifying monster.
Circe's rebuke shows Ulysses as defiant and combative, unwilling to accept defeat even by the gods.
Circe's warning about harming the flocks anticipates the crew's later fate and Ulysses' late, lonely return.
Ulysses withholds the truth to keep his men working, showing his cunning and his willingness to manage others for their own good.
The churning sea is compared to a boiling cauldron, making the whirlpool's violence vivid through a familiar domestic image.
The men crying out Ulysses' name in despair stirs sympathy and shows his guilt as their leader.
The calm fisherman and the helpless fish make the men's death more horrifying by contrasting casual routine with terror.
Eurylochus' accusation that Ulysses is made of iron shows him as a resentful, persuasive agitator who plays on the crew's exhaustion.
Ulysses' oath, demanded because he sees heaven plans mischief, anticipates that the men will break it.
Night "sprang forth out of the heavens" as if a living being, intensifying the sudden violence of the storm.
Ulysses leaves to pray and falls asleep, absent just when his men will break the oath.
Eurylochus calls famine the worst death, yet his choice will bring a worse fate: destruction at the sun's hand.
The crawling hides and lowing meat are supernatural signs of divine anger, warning of the punishment that follows.
The drowning men bobbing in the waves are compared to sea-gulls, making their helplessness vivid and pitiable.
Ulysses clinging to the fig tree like a bat conveys his desperate, dangling position above the whirlpool.
The weary juryman's longing for supper gives Ulysses' relief a homely, human comparison amid the epic danger.
Ulysses' impatience at repeating himself closes his tale in a natural, personal way, reminding us he is speaking to a host.
